sections.sectionText: Introduction to the history of French as a heritage language in African American, Native American, and Cajun American communities in North America from early colonial to late modern times. Focus on the lived experiences and lasting heritage of contact and segregation between colonizers, farmers, refugees, and free and enslaved populations in the American Midwest and South. Taught in English. Online, one synchronous session with the instructor available for discussions on Thursdays from 4-5:20 pm. sections.sectionText: Campus Honors Program: “French Food for Thought”: An exploration of the historical and sociological impact of French food culture on western societies. The course unpacks why French food holds such an important place in western society and how it came to be. It will also look closely at certain food types to understand their prominence in every day cuisine. This section for Chancellor's Scholars only; other students may only enroll with consent of instructor and the Campus Honors Program

sections.sectionText: FR 319 will study foundational francophone theory and literature. We will proceed through many former French colonies and some protectorates (although not all) by advancing chronologically through theory, literature and film. Particular attention will be paid to the theoretical texts from the founders of francophonie. It is the aim of this course to show how historical and political realities of the colonial and post-colonial era are represented in literature and film. The course will end with a look towards the future of post-colonial writings.

sections.sectionText: Contemporary Literature in French: Choix Goncourt US 2026” Come and decide who will be the next winner of the Choix Goncourt US! The Prix Goncourt is one of the most prestigious francophone literary prizes, awarded each year since 1903 by the ten members of the Académie Goncourt in Paris. With the Choix Goncourt, students on campuses across the globe have the opportunity to participate in this competition. This year, our university was selected to be one of nine participating institutions across the US. This is a unique opportunity to practice your analytic and interpretive skills in a collaborative experiential context where you will be a direct contributor to the literary scene – and to the making of francophone culture. In class, we will read the four nominated novels, discuss the role of literary prizes and cultural diplomacy in the creation of cultural value, reflect on best practices as a selection committee, and choose our winner. We will then elect a delegate who will travel to New York City in April to defend our choice, deliberate with the delegates of the other eight participating universities, and vote on the next “Choix Goncourt US”. sections.sectionText: Brussels: Capital of Europe, Capital of Contradictions This advanced half-semester course, including a two-week faculty-led excursion to Brussels and Leuven, offers students an immersive exploration of one of Europe’s most complex and dynamic cities. Through a combination of guided visits, site-based analysis, and structured academic reflection, students will investigate how Brussels functions simultaneously as an officially bi-lingual but mostly Francophone and multilingual national capital, a supranational hub, and a postcolonial space. The course emphasizes direct engagement with the city as a living archive. Students will visit European institutions, museums, and historically significant neighborhoods, while also interacting with local scholars, practitioners, and, where possible, students from KU Leuven.

sections.sectionText: FR 573 Sociabilités au 18e siècle, dans la fiction et les écrits personnels. Selected topics in philosophical and literary works as well as personal texts. The focus will be on the concept of sociability, on the changing representations of social classes or "conditions”, and on the development of new conceptions of the public sphere and the private self in the long eighteenth century. Writers will include Marivaux, Prévost, Graffigny, Diderot, Rousseau, Mercier, Rétif, Charrière, Madame Roland. Course taught in French. Primary readings in French, secondary readings in French and English.

sections.sectionText: FR 576 is a graduate level course that will explore multiple aspects of colonialism through film. We will explore how those in the margins are represented in film—by filmmakers of color. The course will be divided into the following themes: pre-colonization (West Africa), colonization (Antilles, West Africa), the struggle for independence (Maghreb, Central and South Africa), post-colonization/Diaspora (France). Films will be accompanied by the reading of complementary critical articles. The films will be screened in class, with discussion to follow. Course will be conducted in English

sections.sectionText: Remembering and Reimagining HIV/AIDS in Contemporary Times This interdisciplinary course explores HIV/AIDS as both a biomedical condition and a socially constructed phenomenon. Through frameworks that examine the relationship between individuals, society, medicine, and technology, students will analyze how HIV/AIDS has been represented, contested, and experienced across time and space. Drawing from the humanities and social sciences, the course investigates the epidemic’s intersections with race, class, gender, and sexuality, while engaging with activism, policy, and cultural production. Emphasis is placed on critical analysis of historical texts, ethnographies, and media, fostering civic imagination and insight into how health crises reveal broader questions of identity, inequity, and social change.
